answer: STRENGTHS: (1) Real, well-articulated pain point: small cities lack affordable, consistent vacancy data and need it to justify grant applications and measure outcomes. (2) Focused niche: single-purpose product aimed at small cities underserved by large platforms; simplicity and price are credible differentiators. (3) Complementary team: planning domain knowledge (Marcus, with municipal office exposure), statistics/modeling (Priya), and engineering (Tobias). (4) Execution evidence: working prototype, LLC registered, demo to two city offices and a regional planning group, website live, with positive qualitative feedback. (5) Self-awareness and low burn: founders acknowledge gaps (sales, data access, privacy, pricing) and have spent minimal capital. (6) Clear use of funds and a sensible pilot-first go-to-market. WEAKNESSES: (1) Data access is the existential risk: utility data requires agreements with providers who have little incentive to share, and mail-delivery vacancy flags depend on unclear sources (USPS/HUD-type data has licensing and coverage limits). No agreements are in place, and the product cannot scale or even be validated without them. (2) Unvalidated accuracy: no evidence the vacancy score has been checked against ground truth (field surveys, assessor data); a data product's credibility depends on demonstrated precision. (3) No traction signals beyond verbal interest: no LOIs, signed pilots, or paying customers; 'useful' feedback from municipal staff is weak evidence of willingness to pay. (4) Market sizing is hand-waved: 'several hundred cities' at 'low thousands' per year implies a small ceiling (low single-digit millions in revenue at best), a lifestyle-scale business rather than a venture-scale one, with long, slow government sales cycles and tight budgets. (5) Weak defensibility: the method is admittedly not unique; incumbents (CoreLogic, Esri, Cityworks, etc.) or cities' own analysts/universities could replicate it, and the moat is only speed and relationships, which the team lacks. (6) No sales experience on a team selling to local government, the hardest customer segment. (7) Privacy/legal exposure is unresolved; utility usage data is sensitive and regulated, and the claim that property-level aggregation is safe is untested. (8) Student founders with likely part-time commitment, and financial projections admittedly untested (pricing, purchase timing). OVERALL: Compelling problem and sensible, scrappy early execution, but the core data dependency, unproven accuracy, absent customer commitments, and limited market size/defensibility make this a moderate-interest, high-risk early-stage opportunity best suited to small grant/competition-level support and pilot validation rather than meaningful investment now.
